title: 2026-10-14 POC Weekly Sync - Throughput Optimization
summary: Weekly POC sync focusing on throughput tuning for the pilot. Reviewed last week's benchmark (baseline 120 req/s), discussed continuous batching and concurrency levers, decided to run a new benchmark with concurrency raised to 24 and a shorter batching window, and agreed on action items: Diego to run bench, Maya to share updated dashboard and cost estimate, BrightHealth to validate latency SLOs against sampled traffic.
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: all right, good morning everyone, thanks for making time. this is our weekly poc sync for throughput optimization. quick roll call?
[00:07] Lena Park: hi, lena here.
[00:09] Raj Singh: raj here.
[00:11] Emily Carter: emily on as well.
[00:13] Diego Alvarez: diego from redwood engineering.
[00:15] Maya Chen: awesome. quick agenda: recap last week's benchmarks, dig into continuous batching and concurrency, decide next benchmark config, and outline next steps.
[00:25] Maya Chen: Diego, can you walk through the numbers from the test you ran yesterday?
[00:28] Diego Alvarez: yeah, sure. so we ran the synthetic traffic run against the customer's staging workload -- tokens per request skewed small median ~80 tokens. baseline test (no batching, concurrency 8) gave us roughly 120 requests per second at p95 latency ~420ms. with continuous batching enabled and a 40ms max batch window we pushed throughput to ~260 req/s but p95 jumped slightly to ~470ms, which is expected since we were waiting to accumulate micro-batches.
[01:05] Raj Singh: where was GPU util in those runs? we saw some spikes in our dashboard.
[01:10] Diego Alvarez: GPU util averaged 62% in the baseline, with batching it moved to ~78% and occasionally hit low 90s during bursts. memory and KV cache behavior looked fine; cache hit rate around 91% for the prefix-heavy traffic sample.
[01:25] Lena Park: the thing for us is the latency SLO — we target p95 < 500ms for customer-facing flows. so 470ms is okay but we don't want to push much higher. also cost impact is a factor.
[01:38] Maya Chen: good note. Diego, did you test different batching windows?
[01:42] Diego Alvarez: yes. 20ms window gave us ~210 req/s with p95 ~430ms. 60ms pushed to ~300 req/s but p95 crossed 520ms so that's outside your SLO. so tradeoff is there. the other lever is concurrency: increasing concurrent in-flight requests reduces headroom for batching but raises parallelism.
[02:05] Emily Carter: what concurrency did you use with those batching windows?
[02:09] Diego Alvarez: baseline concurrency was 8; the batching experiments used concurrency 16. we also tried concurrency 24 in a short run — that one looked promising: with 24 and a 20ms batch window we saw ~360 req/s and p95 ~480ms, GPU util ~85%.
[02:28] Raj Singh: interesting. so 24 concurrency with 20ms gets us closer to our 500 req/s target if we scale to two pods? how linear is that?
[02:37] Diego Alvarez: roughly linear initially but you'll run into queuing effects and memory limits once you hit the model kv cache saturation. in our lab runs, two pods at that config hit ~700-740 req/s aggregate with p95 ~490-520ms depending on request token variance. so it's feasible but you need to monitor queue lengths and egress latency.
[02:58] Lena Park: memory saturation is my concern — we have long context traces in some flows. does that change the batch behavior?
[03:05] Diego Alvarez: yes, larger contexts increase per-request memory and can reduce effective batch size because of token-length packing. for those long-context cases we suggest route-level policies: small tokens route to high-throughput pool, long-context flows route to dedicated nodes with higher memory but lower concurrency.
[03:20] Maya Chen: that fits with the routing policies we've discussed. any idea about the KV cache warmup time? our production will have cold starts sometimes.
[03:28] Diego Alvarez: kv cache warmup in the bench was fast — within the first few hundred requests hit rates climbed to 85-90%. but cold-start for a new shard can add 50-150ms for the first few requests. we can mitigate with proactive warming if you have predictable prefixes.
[03:43] Emily Carter: ok. about cost — can you give a ballpark for running at the 24 concurrency, two-pod scenario? we need to compare to our current endpoint spend.
[03:51] Diego Alvarez: I'll put numbers in the dashboard, but rough estimate is about 1.8x cost vs the baseline single-pod low-concurrency setup given higher GPU util and more pods. however unit cost per request falls because throughput increases, so depends on your traffic profile. Maya will follow up with a more detailed estimate.
[04:08] Maya Chen: yes i'll share a cost breakdown in the perf sheet.
[04:12] Raj Singh: what about queueing and rate-limiting? we saw some tail latencies spike when traffic burst suddenly.
[04:18] Diego Alvarez: that's typical: if requests enter faster than processing, your request queue grows and p99 spikes. two mitigations: a) front-end rate limiting + token bucket to smooth bursts, b) adaptive concurrency that scales pools when queue length exceeds threshold. both are config knobs in Redwood Dedicated and Redwood Private.
[04:35] Lena Park: do we have support for autoscale at the timescales we need? our traffic bursts are short — 10-30 seconds.
[04:42] Diego Alvarez: autoscale typically acts on a 30s-2m window for cold scale, but we support burst capacity and overprovisioning warm pools for short spikes. we can set policies to keep a small warm buffer to absorb 10-30s spikes.
[04:55] Emily Carter: any known regressions vs other vendors in terms of p95 at these throughputs?
[05:00] Diego Alvarez: from our benchmarks, Redwood's continuous batching with KV cache yields similar or better unit cost vs hosted alternatives like Hugging Face for these open models, and better latency control vs some multi-tenant providers. Lambda Labs is competitive on price but hardware scheduling can cause jitter. runAI (RunAI) gives strong GPU packing but needs extra orchestration.
[05:20] Maya Chen: okay, let's pick the next bench configuration to run. Diego you suggested earlier 24 concurrency + 20ms window, two pods. do we all agree?
[05:28] Raj Singh: yes, run that. also include a mixed traffic pattern with 10% long context requests to see the packing impact.
[05:35] Lena Park: please also capture queue length metrics and p99.
[05:38] Diego Alvarez: noted. i'll run the benchmark with: concurrency 24, batch window 20ms, two pods, mixed traffic load (90/10 short/long contexts), collect p50/p95/p99, GPU util, kv cache hit, and queue length over time.
[05:53] Maya Chen: timeframe? can you have results by next Wednesday?
[05:57] Diego Alvarez: yes, i'll run the bench tomorrow and post results by 2026-10-16 EOD.
[06:02] Maya Chen: great. next, a quick discussion about fallback policies: we talked about model variants for graceful degradation. any decisions?
[06:09] Diego Alvarez: for production we recommend a thirty-second window where if the primary high-accuracy model crosses p95 threshold we route a percentage to a quantized variant that reduces token latency by ~15-25% at slight quality cost. we can automate via rollout policies.
[06:25] Emily Carter: let's plan a small canary for that. Raj, can your team validate quality on the quantized model for a small sample?
[06:31] Raj Singh: yes, we can do a quality pass on 500 random samples once Diego pushes the variant.
[06:36] Maya Chen: perfect. any blockers on the security/compliance front that would affect the bench?
[06:40] Lena Park: we need the audit log for bench runs for our compliance team, and SSO access for their staff to view dashboards.
[06:46] Diego Alvarez: audit logs are enabled in the staging account; i'll make sure the bench includes log exports and grant SSO view access to the BrightHealth group.
[06:54] Maya Chen: ok to summarize next steps?
[06:57] Maya Chen: diego runs bench and posts spreadsheet by 2026-10-16, maya shares cost breakdown and updated perf dashboard by 2026-10-16, brighthealth to run quality validation on quantized variant once available, schedule next sync for 2026-10-21 to review results.
[07:15] Emily Carter: sounds good. thanks everyone.
[07:18] Lena Park: thanks.
[07:20] Raj Singh: thanks.
[07:22] Diego Alvarez: thanks, bye.
action_items: Diego Alvarez; Run benchmark with concurrency=24, batch_window=20ms, two pods, mixed traffic (90/10 short/long); collect p50/p95/p99, GPU util, kv cache hit, queue length; due 2026-10-16
Maya Chen; Share updated performance dashboard and cost breakdown comparing baseline vs 24-concurrency two-pod config; due 2026-10-16
Raj Singh; Run quality validation on quantized model variant for 500 samples once Diego publishes; due 2026-10-20
Diego Alvarez; Enable audit logs and grant SSO view access for BrightHealth staging group; due 2026-10-15

Maya to share cost estimate and recommended autoscale/policy settings by 2026-10-16
Customer to validate quantized variant quality and confirm latency SLO acceptance by 2026-10-20
